title: REG U4·W1 — Property Transactions: Basis, Character & Depreciation Recapture (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — what happens when MBG sells an asset

When Meridian Building Group sells a used excavator or a parcel of land, three questions decide the tax: how much gain or loss is realized, how much is recognized, and what character (ordinary or capital) it carries. REG Unit 1 introduced property transactions; this week works the mechanics at exam depth — basis determination, the capital-gain netting process, the special §1231 rules for business property, and depreciation recapture. All figures use the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline.

Realized versus recognized gain

Gain or loss realized equals the amount realized (cash plus the fair value of property received plus liabilities assumed by the buyer) minus the adjusted basis of the asset given up. Gain recognized is the portion actually taxed — usually equal to realized gain, except where a nonrecognition rule (like the §1031 exchange covered next week) defers it. The first discipline of every property problem is to separate the two: compute the realized amount mechanically, then ask whether any provision limits recognition.

Cost and adjusted basis

Basis begins at cost — what was paid, including debt incurred. It is then increased by capital improvements and decreased by depreciation, depletion, and amortization allowed (or allowable). For MBG's equipment, the adjusted basis is original cost minus accumulated depreciation; for land, basis is cost plus improvements with no depreciation. Getting adjusted basis right is essential because it is the figure subtracted from the amount realized — an overstated basis understates the gain.

Basis of gifted and inherited property

Two transfers receive special basis rules. Gifted property takes a carryover (transferred) basis for computing gain, but for computing a loss the basis is the lower of carryover basis or fair value at the gift date — the dual-basis rule, which can produce no gain or loss if the sale price falls between the two. The donee's holding period tacks (includes the donor's). Inherited property instead takes a stepped-up (or down) basis equal to fair value at the date of death, and its holding period is automatically long-term regardless of how long it is actually held — a powerful planning feature that erases the decedent's unrealized appreciation.

Character: capital versus ordinary

The character of gain drives the rate. A capital asset is defined by exclusion under §1221 — everything except inventory, accounts receivable, and depreciable property or real property used in a trade or business (and a few others). So MBG's inventory of spec homes produces ordinary income, while a personal investment in stock produces capital gain. Long-term treatment requires a holding period of more than one year; one year or less is short-term, taxed at ordinary rates.

Capital gain and loss netting

Capital gains and losses run through a netting process: short-term items net against each other, long-term items net against each other, and the two results are then combined. A net long-term capital gain enjoys preferential rates — 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income — with special rates for unrecaptured §1250 gain (25%) and collectibles (28%), plus the 3.8% net investment income tax for higher earners. A net capital loss for an individual offsets ordinary income only up to $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward indefinitely (corporations carry capital losses back 3 and forward 5, usable only against capital gains).

Section 1231 property

Depreciable property and real property used in a business and held more than one year are §1231 assets — and they get the best of both worlds. At year-end the taxpayer nets all §1231 gains and losses: a net §1231 gain is treated as long-term capital gain (preferential rate), while a net §1231 loss is treated as ordinary (fully deductible). A five-year lookback prevents abuse: a current net §1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary to the extent of net §1231 losses deducted in the prior five years. This is the classification MBG's equipment and buildings fall into.

Depreciation recapture

Before §1231 capital treatment applies, depreciation recapture claws back the benefit of past deductions as ordinary income. §1245 (personal property — equipment, machinery) recaptures all prior depreciation as ordinary income, up to the amount of gain. Worked example: MBG buys an excavator for $100,000, takes $60,000 of depreciation (adjusted basis $40,000), and sells it for $90,000. The $50,000 gain is entirely ordinary because the recapture potential ($60,000) exceeds the gain. §1250 (real property) recaptures only depreciation taken in excess of straight-line — usually zero today since real property uses straight-line — but the prior depreciation becomes unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25%.

A capital-gain netting walkthrough

The netting process rewards careful ordering. Suppose an investor has a $10,000 long-term capital gain, a $4,000 long-term capital loss, a $3,000 short-term capital gain, and a $9,000 short-term capital loss. First net within each group: long-term nets to a $6,000 net long-term gain; short-term nets to a $6,000 net short-term loss. Combining the two leaves $0 — the net short-term loss fully offsets the net long-term gain, and the preferential rate never comes into play. Had the long-term gain been larger, the excess would keep its preferential character; had the short-term loss been larger, up to $3,000 would offset ordinary income with the rest carried forward. Sequencing the buckets correctly is what makes these problems mechanical rather than guesswork.

Personal-use property and casualty losses

Not every asset behaves like an investment. A gain on personal-use property (a personal vehicle, a residence beyond the §121 exclusion) is taxable as a capital gain, but a loss on purely personal-use property is generally nondeductible. Under the 2026 Public Law 119-21 rules, an individual's personal casualty loss remains deductible only when attributable to a federally declared disaster (with state-declared disasters now also recognized under the updated rules), subject to the per-event and AGI floors. This asymmetry — tax the gain, deny the loss — is a recurring trap on personal assets that MBG's owner must remember for his own return.

CMA bridge

The CMA program tracked MBG's equipment basis and depreciation for book purposes; REG shows the tax consequences when that equipment is sold — §1245 recapture turning a seemingly capital gain into ordinary income. The book-versus-tax basis difference is exactly the kind of schedule the CFO must maintain to forecast the tax on an asset sale.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute realized gain (amount realized − adjusted basis); separate realized from recognized.
  2. Apply basis rules: cost (adjusted for improvements/depreciation), gift (carryover for gain, dual-basis for loss, tacked holding period), inheritance (FMV at death, automatically long-term).
  3. Determine character (capital asset by §1221 exclusion; LT requires >1 year), then net capital gains/losses ($3,000 ordinary offset, carryforward).
  4. Apply §1231 (net gain = LTCG, net loss = ordinary, 5-year lookback) after §1245 (full) and §1250 (excess-over-SL; 25% unrecaptured) recapture.

Recap: realized gain is amount realized minus adjusted basis; basis is cost adjusted for improvements and depreciation, carryover-with-dual-basis for gifts, and stepped to FMV (automatically long-term) for inheritances; character turns on the §1221 capital-asset definition and the >1-year holding period, with long-term gains taxed at 0/15/20% (25% unrecaptured §1250, 28% collectibles) and a $3,000 net capital loss offset; and business property is §1231 (net gain = capital, net loss = ordinary, 5-year lookback) only after §1245 recaptures all depreciation as ordinary and §1250 captures excess-over-straight-line — illustrated by MBG's excavator generating $50,000 of fully ordinary recapture income.

flashcards.back: Realized = amount realized (cash + FMV property + liabilities assumed) − adjusted basis. Recognized = the portion taxed (usually = realized unless a nonrecognition rule defers it).
Gain: carryover (donor's) basis. Loss: lower of carryover basis or FMV at gift date. Sale price between the two → no gain or loss. Holding period tacks.
FMV at date of death (stepped up or down); holding period is automatically long-term regardless of actual holding time.
Defined by exclusion: everything EXCEPT inventory, A/R, and depreciable/real property used in a business. Business inventory = ordinary; investments = capital.
0/15/20% by income; unrecaptured §1250 gain 25%; collectibles 28%; plus 3.8% NIIT. Net capital loss offsets ordinary income up to $3,000/yr (carryforward).
Net §1231 gain → long-term capital gain (preferential). Net §1231 loss → ordinary (fully deductible). 5-year lookback recharacterizes current gain as ordinary to the extent of prior §1231 losses.
Personal property (equipment): recaptures ALL prior depreciation as ordinary income, up to the gain. Excess gain above original cost is §1231.
Real property: recaptures only depreciation above straight-line (usually $0). Prior SL depreciation becomes unrecaptured §1250 gain, taxed at a max 25%.

questions.q: Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to:
choices: Fair value at the date of death
The lower of cost or FMV
questions.explain: Inherited property is stepped to FMV at death and is automatically long-term.

questions.q: For gifted property sold at a LOSS, the basis is:
choices: The lower of carryover basis or FMV at the gift date
questions.explain: The dual-basis rule uses the lower of carryover basis or gift-date FMV for losses.

questions.q: MBG's inventory of spec homes, when sold, produces:
questions.explain: Inventory is excluded from the §1221 capital-asset definition, so it is ordinary.

questions.q: Equipment cost $100,000, depreciation $60,000 (basis $40,000), sold for $90,000. The $50,000 gain is:
questions.explain: §1245 recaptures depreciation ($60,000 potential) as ordinary; since gain ($50,000) is less, all of it is ordinary.

questions.q: A net §1231 gain for the year is treated as:
choices: Long-term capital gain (subject to the 5-year lookback)
questions.explain: Net §1231 gain is long-term capital gain; net §1231 loss is ordinary. A 5-year lookback can recharacterize gain as ordinary.

questions.q: An individual's net capital loss offsets ordinary income up to:
choices: $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward
questions.explain: Individuals deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss against ordinary income, carrying forward the rest.

questions.q: Unrecaptured §1250 gain (prior straight-line depreciation on real property) is taxed at a maximum rate of:
questions.explain: Unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
